lead: Fluid motion can be described in two ways. Follow one marked particle and record its path: the Lagrangian view. Stand at fixed points and record the velocity passing each point: the Eulerian view. Mass can also be tracked in two ways. A system is a fixed collection of mass whose boundary moves with the fluid. A control volume is a chosen region of space through which mass flows. Pipes, pumps, turbines and pollution studies all use one or both pairs.
prereq: You need Unit 1: the fluid as a continuum, and the idea of a velocity field.

blocks.text: A fluid has no fixed identity. At every point (x, y, z) and time t, the velocity is a vector V. The list of these vectors over space is the velocity field.
V(x, y, z, t) = u(x, y, z, t) i + v(x, y, z, t) j + w(x, y, z, t) k
blocks.where: V is the velocity vector at a fixed point (x, y, z) at time t, in m/s; u, v, w are its x, y, z components in m/s; i, j, k are unit vectors along x, y, z.

blocks.text: The Eulerian description uses this field. You stand at fixed points and record what passes. A flowmeter clamped to a pipe, a camera watching a point in a channel, and a weather station are Eulerian instruments.

The Lagrangian description follows a marked particle. Label it by its starting position r<sub>0</sub> = (x<sub>0</sub>, y<sub>0</sub>, z<sub>0</sub>). Its path is R(r<sub>0</sub>, t), and its velocity is ∂R/∂t with r<sub>0</sub> held fixed. A drifting buoy, a dye blob and a marked fish follow this view.
Both describe the same motion. The Eulerian field is shorter to write and is the normal engineering view. The Lagrangian path tells where one piece of fluid goes; pathlines are drawn from it.

A system is a fixed collection of mass. Its boundary is a material surface: the same particles stay on it, so no mass crosses. A system can change shape, volume and temperature; its mass stays constant.
A control volume is a chosen region of space. Mass can cross its boundary, the control surface. The control volume may be fixed (a pipe section), moving (a pump impeller), or deforming (a balloon).

Identification: water inside a sealed bottle is a system; water between two flanges of a municipal supply pipe is a control volume. A dye blob released in a river is a system; the river reach between two bridges is a control volume.

Some syllabi call the Eulerian–Lagrangian pair methods of analysis and the mass pair the system–control volume approach. The two devices answer different questions: how does this mass move, or what passes through this region?

Use a control volume for machines and pipes. A pump, turbine, nozzle or pipe bend has a clear inlet and outlet; mass enters and leaves. A pipe junction is a common control volume. The control volume lets you apply mass and momentum balances to the device without tracking every particle. The continuity equation is the mass balance on this region.

Use a system to follow a fixed mass. A pollutant blob, a fuel spray or a cooling parcel is easier as a system. The pollutant mass stays the same; its shape does not. Conservation of mass for a system is simple; Unit 3's Reynolds transport theorem converts system laws into control volume laws.

Steady flow does not mean zero acceleration. In steady flow the field at a fixed point does not change with time (∂V/∂t = 0), but a particle can still accelerate by moving to a place with different velocity. A steady flow through a contracting pipe accelerates the water; the two-part acceleration is in velocity and acceleration of fluid particles.
For a quick check, ask whether the boundary is made of the same particles or is a fixed geometric surface.

spec.title: Two views, two devices
spec.aria: The two description methods, Lagrangian and Eulerian, lead to the two devices, system and control volume.

examples.question: A particle's position is x = 1 + 2t and y = 3t², with x and y in metres and t in seconds. (a) Find the particle velocity and acceleration in the Lagrangian view. (b) Write the Eulerian velocity field by eliminating t. (c) Evaluate the vertical velocity at the point (3, 3).
steps: Differentiate x with respect to t at fixed particle label: u = dx/dt = 2 m/s.
Differentiate again: ax = du/dt = 0 m/s²; ay = dv/dt = 6 m/s².
Eliminate t: t = (x − 1)/2 s. Then v = 6t = 3(x − 1) m/s. The horizontal component is u = 2 m/s everywhere, so V = 2 i + 3(x − 1) j.
At (3, 3), x = 3 m, so v = 3(3 − 1) = 6 m/s. Check: x = 3 gives t = 1 s and y = 3(1)² = 3 m, so the point lies on the path. This Eulerian field has no t, so it is steady, yet ay = 6 m/s² is not zero.
examples.answer: The velocity is u = 2 m/s and v = 6t m/s, the acceleration is ay = 6 m/s², and the vertical velocity at (3, 3) is 6 m/s.
examples.check:
x0 = 1
u = 2
ay = 6
x = 3
t = (x - x0) / 2
v = 6 * t
print(int(u))
print(int(ay))
print(int(v))

traps: Steady flow does not mean zero acceleration. At a fixed point ∂V/∂t = 0, but a particle can accelerate by moving into a region of different velocity; a steady contraction still accelerates water.
The mass inside a control volume is not fixed. Mass can enter and leave; only a system has fixed mass.
A system boundary moves with the fluid; a control surface is a chosen boundary and may be fixed, moving or deforming. Do not use the words as synonyms.
Eulerian is not the same as steady. Eulerian means watch fixed points; the field may change with time.
A control volume need not be fixed in space; a pump impeller or a balloon is a moving or deforming control volume.

quiz.q: State the Eulerian description of fluid motion.
quiz.a: Give the velocity at every fixed point of space as a function of position and time, V(x, y, z, t).

quiz.q: Define a system in fluid mechanics.
quiz.a: A fixed collection of mass whose boundary moves with the fluid; no mass crosses the boundary.

quiz.q: Why is the Eulerian view standard in engineering?
quiz.a: The field at fixed points is easier to measure and gives equations for a chosen region; particles need not be tagged.

quiz.q: Give one difference between a system boundary and a control surface.
quiz.a: A system boundary is a material surface that moves with the same particles; a control surface is a chosen geometric surface that mass may cross.

quiz.q: A field has u = 3 + 2t and v = 4x, in m/s. Find the speed at (2, 1) at t = 1 s.
In steady flow through a contracting pipe, is particle acceleration zero? Justify.
quiz.a: No. ∂V/∂t = 0 at a fixed point, but the water speed rises in the contraction, so a particle accelerates. The convective part is nonzero.

quiz.q: A dye blob is released in a river. To track the blob, system or control volume? To find flow past a bridge pier, which? Explain.
quiz.a: Dye blob: system, because you follow the same mass. Bridge pier: control volume, because water enters and leaves a fixed region around the pier.

beyond: Not for the exam. CFD codes mix both views: a fixed mesh is Eulerian, while sprays, bubbles and sediment are often Lagrangian particles. Particle image velocimetry tracks seeded particles in a laser sheet to build an Eulerian velocity field. Smoothed particle hydrodynamics is fully Lagrangian. Turbomachinery codes use moving control volumes for rotor passages. Search: arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian methods, particle tracking velocimetry, moving control volume.
